topic.name: Modeling Capacitor Charge in RCL Circuits With Second-Order ODEs

question.text:
A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $9\,\textrm{V},$ a resistance of $34\,\Omega,$ a capacitance of $\dfrac{1}{24}\,\textrm{F},$ and an inductance of $L=12\,\textrm{H}.$ Find the steady-state charge for this circuit.

Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.
question.explanation:
The diagram for our circuit is shown below.

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. \[ I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} \]

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops. In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=34\,\Omega.$ So, \[ V_R = 34I = 34\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}. \]

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore, \[ V_C = \dfrac{q}{C} = \dfrac{q}{(1/24)} = 24q. \]

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L = 12\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence, \[ V_L = 12\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = 12\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}\right) = 12\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2}. \]

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is \[ 12\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + 34\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 24q = 9. \]

The steady-state charge is the value that the charge $q(t)$ approaches as $t \to \infty.$ In a stable RCL circuit with a constant electromotive force, the transient response eventually decays to zero, leaving a constant charge.

When the system reaches steady state, the charge $q$ is constant. Consequently, the first and second derivatives of the charge with respect to time are zero: \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} = 0. \]

Substituting these steady-state conditions into the differential equation gives \[ 12(0) + 34(0) + 24q = 9, \] which simplifies to \[ 24q = 9 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q = \dfrac{9}{24} = \dfrac{3}{8}. \]

Physically, this represents the state where the capacitor is fully charged and the current has ceased to flow.

Therefore, the steady-state charge is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\dfrac{3}{8}}$ coulombs.

question.text:
A series RCL circuit has a source electromotive force (EMF) of $9\,\textrm{V},$ a resistance of $45\,\Omega,$ a capacitance of $0.01\,\textrm{F},$ and an inductance of $L=15\,\textrm{H}.$ Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds).

Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.
question.explanation:
We have the following circuit diagram.

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. \[ I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} \]

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=45\,\Omega.$ So, \[ V_R = 45I = 45\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}. \]

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore, \[ V_C = \dfrac{q}{C} = \dfrac{q}{0.01} = 100q. \]

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L = 15\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence, \[ V_L = 15\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = 15\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}\right) = 15\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2}. \]

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

\[ 9 = 45\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 100q + 15\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2}, \]

which gives

\[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + 3\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + \dfrac{20}{3}q = \dfrac{3}{5}. \]

example.title: Constructing an Equation Governing the Charge in an RCL Circuit

question.text:
Find the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ (in coulombs) on the capacitor at time $t$ (in seconds) in the circuit given in the diagram above.

Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.
question.explanation:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $8\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor of resistance $16\,\Omega,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\textrm{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\textrm{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. \[ I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} \]

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=16\,\Omega.$ So, \[ V_R = 16I = 16\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}. \]

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore, \[ V_C = \dfrac{q}{C} = \dfrac{q}{0.25} = 4q. \]

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L = 2\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence, \[ V_L = 2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = 2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}\right) = 2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2}. \]

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

\[ 8= 16\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 4q + 2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2}, \]

which gives

\[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + 8\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 2q = 4. \]

example.title: Constructing an Equation Governing the Charge in an RCL Circuit

question.text:
The charge $q(t),$ in coulombs, in a series RCL circuit is governed by the differential equation \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + 4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 8q = 24. \]

Find the steady-state charge for this circuit.
question.explanation:
The steady-state charge is the value that the charge $q(t)$ approaches as $t \to \infty.$ In a stable RCL circuit with a constant electromotive force, the transient response eventually decays to zero, leaving a constant charge.

When the system reaches steady state, the charge $q$ is constant. Consequently, the first and second derivatives of the charge with respect to time are zero: \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0, \qquad \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} = 0. \]

To find the steady-state charge, we substitute these values into the given differential equation: \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + 4\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 8q = 24 \]

Substituting the steady-state conditions gives \[ 0 + 4(0) + 8q = 24, \] which simplifies to \[ 8q = 24 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q = 3. \]

Physically, this represents the state where the capacitor is fully charged and the current $I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}$ has ceased to flow.

Therefore, the steady-state charge is $\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{3}$ coulombs.

example.title: Finding the Steady-State Capacitor Charge in an RCL Circuit: Constant EMF

question.text:
Consider the RCL circuit shown above. Given that the charge $q(t)$ of the capacitor at time $t$ seconds is given by \[ q(t) = Ae^{-2t} + Be^{-t} + \dfrac{P}{10}\cos(2t) + \dfrac{Q}{10}\sin(2t) \] where $A,$ $B,$ $P,$ and $Q$ are constants, find the value of $P + Q.$

Hint: The voltage drop $V_C$ across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C,$ where $C$ is the capacitance measured in Farads.
question.explanation:
The diagram shows a series RCL circuit with a source electromotive force (EMF) of $4\sin(2t)\,\textrm{V},$ a resistor of resistance $6\,\Omega,$ a capacitor of capacitance $0.25\,\textrm{F},$ and an inductor of inductance $2\,\textrm{H}.$

The current $I,$ measured in amperes, is defined as the rate of flow of charge $q,$ measured in coulombs. \[ I = \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} \]

Kirchhoff's voltage law states that in a series circuit, the source voltage (EMF) equals the sum of the voltage drops.

In an RCL circuit, there are three voltage drops:

  • The voltage drop across the resistor is proportional to the current, with a constant of proportionality $R=6\,\Omega.$ So, \[ V_R = 6I = 6\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}. \]

  • The voltage drop across the capacitor is related to its charge by $q = CV_C.$ Therefore, \[ V_C = \dfrac{q}{C} = \dfrac{q}{0.25} = 4q. \]

  • The voltage drop across the inductor is proportional to the rate of change of current, with a constant of proportionality $L = 2\,\textrm{H}.$ Hence, \[ V_L = 2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t} = 2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\left(\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t}\right) = 2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2}. \]

Therefore, by Kirchhoff's voltage law, the differential equation governing the amount of charge $q$ on the capacitor is

\[ 4\sin(2t) = 6\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 4q + 2\,\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2}, \]

which gives

\[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + 3\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q}{\mathrm{d}t} + 2q = 2\sin(2t). \]

The given equation is a second-order linear equation with constant coefficients. To find the general solution, we must sum the complementary and particular solutions.

  • To find the complementary solution $q_c,$ we solve the corresponding homogeneous equation, given by \[ \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q_c}{\mathrm{d}t^2} + 3\cdot\dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_c}{\mathrm{d}t} + 2q_c = 0. \] Solving using an integration technique, such as a trial solution, we obtain the complementary solution \[ q_c(t) = Ae^{-2t} + Be^{-t}, \] where $A$ and $B$ are constants.

  • Next, we find the particular solution. Note that the right-hand side of the inhomogeneous equation is sinusoidal with argument $2t.$ So, we assume that the particular solution is also a sinusoidal with argument $2t,$ i.e., \[ q_p(t) = \alpha\cos(2t) + \beta\sin(2t). \]

    To find the values of $\alpha$ and $\beta,$ we substitute \begin{align*} q_p &= \alpha\cos(2t) + \beta\sin(2t), \\[5pt] \dfrac{\mathrm{d}q_p}{\mathrm{d}t} &= -2\alpha\sin(2t) + 2\beta\cos(2t), \\[5pt] \dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2q_p}{\mathrm{d}t^2} &= -4\alpha\cos(2t) - 4\beta\sin(2t), \end{align*} into the inhomogeneous equation and group like terms on the left-hand side: \begin{align*} \!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\! (-4\alpha\cos(2t) - 4\beta\sin(2t)) + 3(-2\alpha\sin(2t) + 2\beta\cos(2t)) \quad\qquad\qquad& \\ + 2(\alpha\cos(2t) + \beta\sin(2t)) &= 2\sin(2t) \\[5pt] (-2\alpha + 6\beta)\cos(2t) + (-6\alpha - 2\beta)\sin(2t) &= 2\sin(2t) \\[5pt] \end{align*}

    Equating the coefficients, we get the following system of equations: \[ \begin{cases} -2\alpha + 6\beta = 0 \quad&(\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\cos(2t)) \\[5pt] -6\alpha - 2\beta = 2 \quad&(\text{equating the coefficients of}\,\sin(2t)) \end{cases} \]

    Solving this system gives $\alpha = -\dfrac{3}{10},$ $\beta = -\dfrac{1}{10}.$ Therefore, the particular solution is \[ q_p(t) = -\dfrac3{10}\cos(2t) - \dfrac1{10}\sin(2t). \]

Now, since the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary solution and the particular solution, the general solution in our case is \[ q(t) = q_c(t) + q_p(t) = Ae^{-2t} + Be^{-t} - \dfrac3{10}\cos(2t) - \dfrac1{10}\sin(2t). \]

Therefore, we have $P=-3,$ $Q=-1,$ and \[ P + Q = -3 + (-1) = -4. \]
